claim: Animal behavior and neural recordings show that the brain is able to measure both the intensity and the timing of odor encounters.
source: Animal behavior and neural recordings show that the brain is able to measure both the intensity and the timing of odor encounters.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on animal behavior and neural recordings, as indicated in the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: Most macroscopic organisms detect odors in intermittent bursts, that may be separated by extended regions with no odor.
source: Most macroscopic organisms detect odors in intermittent bursts, that may be separated by extended regions with no odor.
evidence: This is a general statement about olfactory detection patterns supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Organisms leverage intermittent odor dynamics efficiently for diverse tasks, including locating and identifying an odor source.
source: Organisms leverage this complex dynamics efficiently for diverse tasks, including locating and identifying an odor source Murlis et al., 1992; Mafra-Neto and Cardé, 1994; Vickers, 2000; Riffell et al., 2014; Ache et al., 2016; Ackels et al., 2021.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Behavioral evidence suggests that animals use both intensity and timing of odor encounters for olfactory navigation.
source: Behavioral evidence suggests that animals use both intensity and timing of odor encounters for olfactory navigation Baker et al., 2018.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baker et al., 2018.

claim: At close range, mammals appear to compare odor intensity either across nostrils or across sniffs.
source: At close range, mammals appear to compare odor intensity either across nostrils or across sniffs Catania, 2013; Gire et al., 2016; Findley et al., 2021.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies on mammalian olfaction.

claim: Timing of odor detection plays a key role for olfactory navigation.
source: On the other hand, mounting evidence suggests timing of odor detection also plays a key role for olfactory navigation Ache et al., 2016
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ache et al., 2016.

claim: Moths respond to odor pulsed at specific frequencies.
source: moths respond to odor pulsed at specific frequencies Riffell et al., 2014; Vickers et al., 2001
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies on moth behavior.

claim: Fruit flies respond to timing since last odor detection.
source: fruit flies respond to timing since last odor detection van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014; Demir et al., 2020
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies on fruit fly behavior.

claim: Lobsters and sharks compare odor arrival time across their paired olfactory organs and orient toward the side that detected the odor first.
source: lobsters and sharks compare odor arrival time across their paired olfactory organs and orient toward the side that detected the odor first Basil and Atema, 1994; Gardiner and Atema, 2010
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies on lobster and shark olfaction.

claim: Many organisms will move upwind upon detection of an odor.
source: many organisms will move upwind upon detection of an odor Kennedy and Marsh, 1974; Murlis et al., 1992; Steck et al., 2012.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies on organism behavior.

claim: The brain of many animals is able to record information both about intensity (and its derivatives) as well as timing of odor encounters.
source: Neural recordings upon stimulation with intermittent odor cues confirm that the brain of many animals is able to record information both about intensity (and its derivatives) as well as timing of odor encounters (most information comes from work on arthropods Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Vickers et al., 2001; Brown et al., 2005; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Jacob et al., 2017; Riffell et al., 2014, but see also Parabucki et al., 2019; Lewis et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to neural recording studies.

claim: When insects are presented with intermittent odor cues, information about intensity and timing is recorded in their antennal lobe.
source: For example, when insects are presented with intermittent odor cues, information about intensity and timing is recorded in their antennal lobe (see e.g. Vickers et al., 2001; Brown et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies on insect antennal lobe recordings.

claim: Odors that mimic natural intermittency elicit a response that preserves an accurate measure of timing in fruit flies and moths.
source: Odors that mimic natural intermittency elicit a response that preserves an accurate measure of timing in fruit flies and moths Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Jacob et al., 2017.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies on fruit fly and moth responses.

claim: In lobsters, bursting olfactory neurons encode specifically for the time between successive odor encounters.
source: In lobsters, bursting olfactory neurons encode specifically for the time between successive odor encounters, see Park et al., 2014; Park et al., 2016 and references therein.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies on lobster olfactory neurons.

claim: The neural activity varies considerably with the dynamics of the odor cues.
source: Interestingly, the neural activity varies considerably with the dynamics of the odor cues Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Vickers et al., 2001; Lewis et al., 2021
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies on neural activity.

claim: Turbulence causes the odor to be distributed in highly intermittent patches separated by blanks with no odor.
source: Indeed, we know from theoretical Shraiman and Siggia, 2000; Falkovich et al., 2001; Celani et al., 2014 and experimental Justus et al., 2002; Moore and Crimaldi, 2004 work that turbulence causes the odor to be distributed in highly intermittent patches separated by blanks with no odor.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to both theoretical and experimental studies.

claim: Both intensity and timing of intermittent bursts vary depending on the location of the source.
source: Both intensity and timing of these intermittent bursts vary depending on the location of the source Celani et al., 2014
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Celani et al., 2014.

claim: Measures of odor temporal dynamics based on a short memory span (down to about 1 s) hold information about source location.
source: We find that measures of odor temporal dynamics based on a short memory span (down to about 1 s) hold information about source location.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Close to the source or close to the substrate, measures of intensity predict distance better than measures of timing.
source: Close to the source or close to the substrate, measures of intensity predict distance better than measures of timing
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ranking of intensity versus timing features is reversed at further distance from the source or from the substrate.
source: but this ranking is reversed at further distance from the source or from the substrate.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pairing timing and intensity features improves dramatically the quality of the prediction robustly across all datasets.
source: Pairing the two kinds of measure improves dramatically the quality of the prediction robustly across all datasets
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pairing two measures of intensity or two measures of timing is either useless or detrimental.
source: whereas pairing two measures of intensity or two measures of timing is either useless or detrimental.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Timing and intensity are complementary attributes of odor dynamics.
source: Our results demonstrate that timing and intensity are complementary attributes of odor dynamics
evidence: This claim is inferred from the machine learning analysis results showing that combining timing and intensity features improves predictions.

claim: Timing features are most effective in more dilute conditions.
source: and are most effective in more dilute and concentrated conditions respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intensity features are most effective in more concentrated conditions.
source: and are most effective in more dilute and concentrated conditions respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: For the dataset at source height, intensity features rank higher than timing features.
source: For this dataset, intensity features rank higher than timing features (Figure 2b–c)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2b-c.

claim: Predictions are more accurate in the crosswind than in the downwind direction.
source: and predictions are more accurate in the crosswind than in the downwind direction (compare with Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Performance at source height varies little over the three source locations.
source: Performance at source height varies little over the three locations, demonstrating that the algorithm is learning the dynamics of the scalar and not of the carrying flow (see Figure 2—figure supplement 5 center).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 center.

claim: Irrespective of source position, timing features acquire predictive power with height.
source: Additionally we demonstrate that, irrespective of source position, timing features acquire predictive power with height
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 right.

claim: Intensity features lose predictive power with height.
source: whereas the opposite is observed for intensity features (see Figure 2—figure supplement 5 right).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 right.

claim: Performance of individual features varies little when test and training are performed over different datasets.
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 6 shows that performance of individual features varies little when test and training are performed over different dataset.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Performance improves with longer memory.
source: Performance improves with longer memory (Figure 3a)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Improvement in performance with memory follows a slow power law.
source: But improvement follows a slow power law so that waiting for example 20 times longer yields predictions only about twice as precise.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Sampling more frequently than once per Kolmogorov time does not essentially affect the results nor ranking.
source: Finally, sampling more frequently than once per Kolmogorov time does not essentially affect the results nor ranking (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Pairing two features of the same category results in little to no improvement.
source: In fact, pairing two features of the same category results in little to no improvement (Figure 4 and similarly for the crosswind direction, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Combining one intensity and one timing feature improves performance considerably, up to 65%.
source: In contrast, combining one intensity and one timing feature improves performance considerably, up to 65%.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Intensity features perform well in locations where timing features perform poorly.
source: This result can be understood by mapping the error done by individual features in space (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), showing that intensity and timing features are complementary, that is intensity features perform well in locations where timing features perform poorly.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: From datasets a to e, sparsity increases and intensity decreases.
source: From a to e, sparsity increases and intensity decreases (Figure 5b)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Closer to the boundary, the air slows down and the odor accumulates.
source: simply because closer to the boundary, the air slows down and the odor accumulates.
evidence: This is based on established fluid dynamics principles.

claim: The two intensity features outperform all timing features when the dataset is not very sparse (dataset a-b).
source: The two intensity features outperform all timing features when the dataset is not very sparse (dataset a-b, Figure 5c and d left).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5c and d left.

claim: Two timing features (intermittency factor and blank duration) outperform all others for the more sparse and less intense dataset d-e.
source: In contrast, two timing features (intermittency factor and blank duration) outperform all others for the more sparse and less intense dataset d-e (Figure 5c and d right).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5c and d right.

claim: Whiff duration performs poorly in d-e because intermittency is too severe and whiffs are short in duration thus bear little information.
source: Whiff duration performs poorly in d-e because intermittency is too severe and whiffs are short in duration thus bear little information (the average whiff duration is 1–7 time steps in over 90% of the time series).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and inference about the relationship between whiff duration and intermittency.

claim: Pairing one intensity and one timing feature remains the most successful strategy across all heights.
source: Although the ranking of individual features shifts with height, pairing one intensity and one timing feature remains the most successful strategy across all heights (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5c and d.

claim: Combining all five features contributes little improvement over mixed pairs.
source: In contrast, combining all five features contributes little improvement (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The odor is more intense and more sparse closer to the source.
source: The odor is more intense and more sparse closer to the source and it becomes more dilute and less sparse with distance from the source (Figure 6b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Performance of individual features degrades with distance.
source: Performance of individual features degrades with distance (Figure 6d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Intensity features clearly outperform timing features at close range.
source: Intensity features clearly outperform timing features at close range, as seen both from various percentiles of the test error (Figure 6d, left) as well as the full distribution (Figure 6c, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6c and 6d left.

claim: The disparity between timing and intensity features disappears in the distal problem.
source: The disparity between timing and intensity features disappears in the distal problem: the error distribution for all individual features is essentially superimposed except for the tails (Figure 6c, right and inset)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6c right and inset.

claim: Mixed pairs outperform all individual features in both the distal and proximal problems.
source: Remarkably, mixed pairs outperform all individual features in both the distal and proximal problems (Figure 6c–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6c-d.

claim: Measuring timing of odor encounters is most useful in regions where the odor is dilute, that is far from the source and from the substrate.
source: Namely, measuring timing of odor encounters is most useful in regions where the odor is dilute, that is far from the source and from the substrate
evidence: This claim is supported by the aggregate of machine learning analysis results.

claim: Measuring intensity is most useful in concentrated conditions, that is close to the source or the substrate.
source: whereas measuring intensity is most useful in concentrated conditions, that is close to the source or the substrate.
evidence: This claim is supported by the aggregate of machine learning analysis results.

claim: The concentration and the slope of a turbulent odor signal, averaged over a memory lag, are particularly useful to predict source location at close range or near the boundary.
source: We find that the concentration and the slope of a turbulent odor signal, averaged over a memory lag, are particularly useful to predict source location at close range or near the boundary.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results.

claim: The primacy of the intensity features wanes in more challenging conditions, for example moving away from the source or away from the boundary.
source: The primacy of the intensity features wanes in more challenging conditions, for example moving away from the source or away from the boundary.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results.

claim: In portions of space where the odor is scarcer, features that quantify timing of odor detection become as effective as intensity features, or more effective.
source: In these portions of space, where the odor is scarcer, features that quantify timing of odor detection become as effective as intensity features, or more effective.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results.

claim: Olfactory receptor neurons in insects appear to encode efficiently information about timing across a wide range of intensities.
source: Interestingly, olfactory receptor neurons in insects appear to encode efficiently information about timing across a wide range of intensities Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Martelli et al., 2013.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies on insect olfactory receptor neurons.

claim: Even within a single flow, odor dynamics and the best predictors vary considerably in space.
source: here we keep all of these parameters constant and demonstrate that even within a single flow, odor dynamics and the best predictors vary considerably in space.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results showing spatial variation in feature performance.

claim: Sparse odor cues elicit individual responses in mice that follow closely the ups and downs of the odor in time.
source: Specifically, sparse odor cues elicit individual responses that follow closely the ups and downs of the odor in time.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Lewis et al., 2021 in the broader context.

claim: Continuous signals elicit intense responses in mice which are however uncorrelated to the temporal dynamics of the odor itself.
source: In contrast, continuous signals elicit intense responses which are however uncorrelated to the temporal dynamics of the odor itself Lewis et al., 2021.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lewis et al., 2021.

claim: Features within the same class are redundant whereas features from different classes are complementary.
source: We find that features within the same class are redundant whereas features from different classes are complementary.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results.

claim: Features of the same class have similar patterns of performance in space, but each class has a distinct pattern.
source: Indeed, features of the same class have similar patterns of performance in space, but each class has a distinct pattern.
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial analysis of feature performance.

claim: Measuring both timing and intensity is beneficial, but using more than one feature to quantify either timing or intensity provides no advantage.
source: As a consequence, measuring both timing and intensity is beneficial, but using more than one feature to quantify either timing or intensity provides no advantage.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results on feature combinations.

claim: Mixed time/intensity pairs of features outrank individual features robustly, that is in all portions of space, regardless of distance from the source and from the ground.
source: Importantly, mixed time/intensity pairs of features outrank individual features robustly, that is in all portions of space, regardless of distance from the source and from the ground.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results across different spatial regions.

claim: Relying on simultaneous timing and intensity features is advantageous when odors are sensed at various distances from the source and from the substrate.
source: This is in contrast with individual features and suggests relying on simultaneous timing and intensity features is advantageous when odors are sensed at various distances from the source and from the substrate.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the robust performance of mixed pairs across different spatial conditions.

claim: The coexistence of bursting olfactory neurons and canonical olfactory neurons in lobsters suggests these animals are able to measure simultaneously timing and intensity.
source: Interestingly, the coexistence of bursting olfactory neurons and canonical olfactory neurons in lobsters suggests these animals are in fact able to measure simultaneously timing and intensity Park et al., 2014; Ache et al., 2016
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies on lobster olfactory neurons.

claim: In mammals, optogenetic activation of the olfactory bulb demonstrates that both kinds of measures guide behavior.
source: Similarly, in mammals, optogenetic activation of the olfactory bulb Smear et al., 2013 demonstrates that both kinds of measures guide behavior (lick vs no lick).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smear et al., 2013.

claim: Binary representations were suboptimal in all conditions considered in Victor et al., 2019; Boie et al., 2018, that is at few tens of cm from the source.
source: (i) binary representations were suboptimal in all conditions considered in Victor et al., 2019; Boie et al., 2018, that is at few tens of cm from the source.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Victor et al., 2019 and Boie et al., 2018.

claim: Individual snapshots of odor from Victor et al., 2019; Boie et al., 2018 contained 1–2 bits of information about source location.
source: (ii) Individual snapshots of odor from Victor et al., 2019; Boie et al., 2018 contained 1–2 bits of information about source location
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Victor et al., 2019 and Boie et al., 2018.

claim: Allocating more resources to represent how the odor varies in time was found informative.
source: but allocating more resources to represent how the odor varies in time was found informative Victor et al., 2019; Boie et al., 2018.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Victor et al., 2019 and Boie et al., 2018.

claim: Mixed pairs of features at close range achieve precisions of 5–6%, corresponding to coding for position with words of 4–4.3 bits.
source: Our mixed pairs of features at close range achieve precisions of 5–6%, corresponding to coding for position with words of 4–4.3 bits.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results and calculation.

claim: Memory is useful for source localization, but the gain does not increase indefinitely with further memory.
source: Our results thus confirm that memory is indeed useful, but the gain does not increase indefinitely with further memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of memory effects shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Both intensity and timing appear to have a potential to lead to an odor source.
source: Overall, both intensity and timing appear to have a potential to lead to an odor source, consistent with our results on individual features.
evidence: This claim is supported by the machine learning analysis results and citations to navigation literature.

claim: A combination of timing and intensity features was found beneficial in Leathers et al., 2020.
source: A combination of the two kinds of features was found beneficial in Leathers et al., 2020, consistent with our results on mixed pairs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leathers et al., 2020.

claim: Timing features are more robust than intensity features with respect to the intensity of the source.
source: Timing features are more robust than intensity features with respect to the intensity of the source and may thus be favored regardless of their performance, which was argued in Schmuker et al., 2016.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schmuker et al., 2016.

claim: Timing features are precisely invariant with source intensity because the detection threshold is defined adaptively.
source: In our work, timing features are precisely invariant with source intensity because we define the detection threshold adaptively (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is based on the methodological choice made in the study.

claim: Within each element the solution is expanded in 8th grade tensor-product polynomials so that the domain is effectively discretized in 81,920,000 elements.
source: within each element the solution is expanded in 8th grade tensor-product polynomials so that the domain is effectively discretized in 81 920,000 elements.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the numerical simulation.

claim: Each DNS requires 2 weeks of computational time using 320 cpus.
source: Each DNS requires 2 weeks of computational time using 320 cpus.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the computational requirements.

claim: Kernel methods are a more powerful class of nonlinear models than linear models for this problem.
source: To tackle this issue, we consider kernel methods Schölkopf and Smola, 2002, a more powerful class of nonlinear models
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citation to Schölkopf and Smola, 2002.

claim: The choice of linear models has limited predictive power and does not allow to rank features.
source: In Figure 2—figure supplement 1, we show that the choice of linear models has limited predictive power and does not allow to rank features.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The precise value of the relative threshold has little effect on the results.
source: The precise value of the relative threshold has little effect on the results as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, left.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, left.

claim: Fixed thresholds were tested and discarded because results depend sensibly on the threshold and the optimal threshold varies with the dataset in non-trivial ways.
source: Fixed thresholds were tested and discarded because results depend sensibly on the threshold and the optimal threshold varies with the dataset in non-trivial ways (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, right.
